claims.text: Incremental Ti addition increases lattice misfit in a Mo-based high-entropy alloy.
Increased lattice misfit produces stronger local strain fields around Ti solute atoms.
The Ti-induced strain fields raise the barrier or critical stress for edge-dislocation motion.
Impeded edge-dislocation glide increases resistance to plastic deformation through solid-solution strengthening.
Increasing Ti content will increase yield strength relative to a low-Ti baseline.
Increasing Ti content will increase nanoindentation hardness relative to a low-Ti baseline.
Edge-dislocation-controlled strengthening becomes important only after lattice misfit or Ti content passes a threshold.
The proposed edge-dislocation mechanism governs strengthening over a moderate range of Ti additions.
Beyond a critical Ti content, secondary phases or phase instability may appear.
Beyond a critical Ti content, the solid-solution strengthening benefit may saturate.
Alternative deformation mechanisms may dominate beyond the proposed Ti or lattice-misfit boundary.
The low-Ti baseline Mo-based HEA is a uniform single-phase solid solution.
The low-Ti baseline has relatively low lattice misfit.
Low-Ti compositions are governed primarily by conventional, rather than edge-controlled, dislocation behavior.
Screw-dislocation motion controls strength at lower Ti concentrations, whereas edge-dislocation strengthening becomes comparable at high Ti concentrations.
XRD and calorimetry can verify that measured strengthening is caused solely by solid-solution effects rather than secondary phases.
A controlled atmosphere at room temperature will avoid oxidation during the experiments.

contradictions.description: The conditions require all tested Ti levels to remain below the phase-segregation threshold, while the predicted outcome proposes observing deviations at that threshold, including phase changes, to define the validity boundary. A series confined below the threshold cannot directly reveal a phase-change boundary.

The intervention seeks to ensure that property changes are solely due to solid-solution effects, and the falsification rule treats strengthening associated with secondary phases as falsifying. The boundary, however, anticipates secondary-phase formation as an expected limitation. The design does not clearly distinguish falsification within the asserted domain from expected failure outside it.
